text: Good morning everyone, let us begin today's lecture on sorting algorithms and their time complexity analysis.
Today we will cover bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort in detail.
Before we start I want to remind you that the assignment on searching algorithms is due this Friday.
A sorting algorithm takes an unsorted array as input and produces a sorted array as output.
The efficiency of a sorting algorithm is measured using time complexity and space complexity.
Time complexity tells us how the running time of an algorithm grows as the size of the input n increases.
We express time complexity using Big O notation where O(n) means linear time and O(n squared) means quadratic time.
An algorithm with O(n squared) complexity becomes very slow for large inputs because the running time grows quadratically.
Let us start with bubble sort which is the simplest sorting algorithm to understand.
In bubble sort we repeatedly compare adjacent elements and swap them if they are in the wrong order.
After each pass through the array the largest unsorted element bubbles up to its correct position.
We need n minus 1 passes through the array of n elements to guarantee the array is fully sorted.
In the worst case bubble sort performs n squared divided by 2 comparisons giving it O(n squared) time complexity.
The best case for bubble sort is when the array is already sorted and we get O(n) time with an early termination flag.
Bubble sort has O(1) space complexity because it sorts the array in place using only a constant amount of extra memory.
Despite its simplicity bubble sort is rarely used in practice because O(n squared) is too slow for large datasets.
Now let us move to merge sort which uses the divide and conquer paradigm to achieve better time complexity.
The divide and conquer approach works by breaking the problem into smaller subproblems solving each recursively and combining the results.
Merge sort divides the array into two halves recursively sorts each half and then merges the two sorted halves.
The merge operation takes two sorted subarrays and combines them into a single sorted array in O(n) time.
The recurrence relation for merge sort is T(n) equals 2 times T(n divided by 2) plus O(n) for the merge step.
Solving this recurrence using the master theorem gives us T(n) equals O(n log n) for merge sort.
This is a significant improvement over O(n squared) because n log n grows much more slowly than n squared for large n.
For example for n equals one million O(n squared) requires one trillion operations while O(n log n) requires only twenty million.
The disadvantage of merge sort is its space complexity which is O(n) because we need auxiliary arrays during the merge step.
This O(n) auxiliary space can be a problem when sorting very large datasets that barely fit in memory.
The master theorem is a tool for solving recurrence relations of the form T(n) equals a times T(n divided by b) plus f(n).
In the master theorem a is the number of subproblems b is the factor by which the input size is reduced and f(n) is the cost of dividing and combining.
There are three cases in the master theorem depending on how f(n) compares to n raised to the power of log base b of a.
For merge sort a equals 2 and b equals 2 so log base 2 of 2 equals 1 and f(n) equals O(n) which matches case 2.
Case 2 of the master theorem gives us T(n) equals O(n log n) confirming our earlier analysis of merge sort.
Now let us examine quick sort which is the most widely used sorting algorithm in practice.
Quick sort also uses divide and conquer but its approach is different from merge sort.
Quick sort selects a pivot element and partitions the array into two parts elements less than the pivot and elements greater than the pivot.
The partition step rearranges the array in place so that the pivot is in its final sorted position.
After partitioning quick sort recursively sorts the left subarray and the right subarray independently.
The performance of quick sort depends heavily on the choice of pivot because a bad pivot choice leads to unbalanced partitions.
In the worst case when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element the recurrence is T(n) equals T(n minus 1) plus O(n).
This worst case recurrence gives O(n squared) time complexity which is as bad as bubble sort.
The worst case occurs when the input array is already sorted and we always pick the first element as the pivot.
In the average case with a good pivot choice the recurrence is T(n) equals 2 times T(n divided by 2) plus O(n).
This is the same recurrence as merge sort giving O(n log n) average case time complexity for quick sort.
To avoid the worst case we use randomised quick sort which selects the pivot randomly from the array.
With random pivot selection the probability of consistently picking a bad pivot becomes negligibly small.
Quick sort has O(log n) average space complexity due to the recursive call stack depth.
This is better than merge sort's O(n) space which is why quick sort is preferred for memory constrained environments.
In practice quick sort is faster than merge sort on real hardware due to better cache locality and fewer memory allocations.
Cache locality means the data being accessed is more likely to already be in the CPU cache leading to fewer expensive memory fetches.
Let us now compare the three algorithms we have studied in terms of their time and space complexity.
Bubble sort has O(n squared) worst and average case time O(n) best case and O(1) space complexity.
Merge sort has O(n log n) in all cases best worst and average which makes it predictably efficient.
Quick sort has O(n log n) average case O(n squared) worst case and O(log n) average space complexity.
The guarantee of O(n log n) in all cases makes merge sort preferable when predictable performance is required.
Quick sort's better cache performance makes it faster in practice despite the theoretical worst case risk.
For exam purposes you should remember that no comparison based sorting algorithm can do better than O(n log n) in the worst case.
This lower bound of Omega(n log n) is proven using a decision tree argument where each comparison is a node in a binary tree.
A binary tree with n factorial leaves representing all possible permutations of n elements must have height at least log base 2 of n factorial.
By Stirling's approximation log of n factorial is approximately n log n proving the lower bound.
This means merge sort and quick sort on average are asymptotically optimal comparison based sorting algorithms.
Non comparison based algorithms like counting sort and radix sort can beat this bound but only under specific assumptions about the input.
Counting sort achieves O(n plus k) where k is the range of input values but requires O(k) extra space.
If k is very large counting sort becomes impractical because the space requirement exceeds what is available.
That is all for today. We will continue with heap sort and radix sort in the next class.
